description_ru: Дождливый июнь в Киото: мох в храмовых садах, камни, которые невозможно увидеть все сразу, чайная церемония и урок о том, что красота любит тишину и терпение.
text:
It rains in Kyoto in June, and it does so with a thoroughness that the guidebooks mention in a single, apologetic sentence, as one might refer to an eccentric aunt. The rainy season, tsuyu, means "plum rain", because it coincides with the ripening of plums, and the name, like most things in Japan, makes a gentle euphemism out of what is, frankly, a prolonged drenching. I arrived in the middle of it with a collapsible umbrella and a hopeful attitude, both of which were defeated by the second afternoon.

The tourists, thank heaven, had mostly fled. The great temples of the old capital, which in April are besieged by blossom-hunters, stood in the wet with an air of exhausted relief, and I wandered into them as into a theatre between performances. At Fushimi Inari, the shrine of thousands of vermilion gates, I climbed the slope through a tunnel of orange pillars, one pace behind a solitary priest in white, while the rain drummed on the wooden roofs and the cedar forest steamed on either side. The gates were donated by merchants hoping for prosperity, each inscribed with a name and a date, and walking beneath them had the odd sensation of being stitched, slowly, through the eye of an enormous needle.

Kyoto was the imperial capital of Japan for more than a thousand years, from 794 until the court moved to Tokyo in 1868, and it was mercifully spared the bombing that destroyed so many cities in the war. The consequence is a place in which an astonishing density of temples, shrines and teahouses has survived, some seventeen of them recognised by UNESCO. Yet it is not a museum. Women in indigo kimono hurried past on bicycles, salarymen sheltered in doorways with their phones, and a convenience store on the corner sold, among its rice balls, an astonishing selection of umbrellas, transparent as soap bubbles, which the entire city seemed to carry.

Even the famous Golden Pavilion, Kinkaku-ji, which I visited in a downpour, proved to be better in bad weather. Its upper floors are covered in gold leaf, and it stands at the edge of a mirror pond, doubling itself in the water with a vanity that the Japanese, uniquely, have elevated to a philosophy. The building one sees is, in fact, a reconstruction, since a disturbed young novice burned the original to the ground in 1950, an event that later inspired a celebrated novel. The replica is exquisite, and the rain, falling in tiny rings upon the pond, shivered the golden reflection into a thousand shifting flakes, as though the pavilion were being gently, and very slowly, melted.

The rain, I soon learned, was not an obstacle to beauty but its collaborator. At Saihō-ji, the so-called moss temple, which requires visitors to apply in advance and, before entering, to copy out a sutra with a brush, the garden is carpeted in more than a hundred varieties of moss. In dry weather they are a muted olive. In the rain they become a startling, jewelled green, deep as velvet and bright as a traffic light, and the little paths wander through them with a sort of apologetic grace. I copied out my sutra with the confidence of a man defusing a bomb, producing a page that the monk who collected it received with the weary tolerance of a teacher reading a child's first essay.

The next day I visited Ryōan-ji, which houses the most famous rock garden in the world. It is, on paper, a laughable proposition: a rectangle of raked white gravel, about the size of a tennis court, containing fifteen stones arranged in clusters, with moss at their feet and nothing else whatever. Visitors sit on a wooden veranda and contemplate it. Nobody knows who made it, or what it means. Some say it is a tiger and her cubs crossing the sea, others an archipelago, others an exercise in pure abstraction. There is an old observation, cherished by every guide, that from any position on the veranda, one of the fifteen stones is always hidden from view, and that only the enlightened may see them all.

I tested this proposition, with the sceptical rigour of a physicist, by shuffling along the veranda from end to end and counting. I counted fourteen, every time. I will not pretend that I attained enlightenment. But as I sat there in the drizzle, with a small crowd of strangers all silent, and the gravel's raked lines seemed to move with the shifting light, I became aware of a curious relief, as if my mind, like the garden, had been raked into order. Nothing was happening. It was wonderful.

In the afternoon, on the recommendation of the innkeeper at my ryokan, a small guesthouse with sliding paper doors, I attended a tea ceremony in a house near Gion. The hostess, a tiny woman of immense gravity, moved around the room like water, whisking powdered green tea in a bowl with a bamboo whisk until it frothed the colour of new leaves. Every gesture was prescribed: the way the bowl was turned, the way it was offered, the way I was meant to turn it again before drinking. I executed these with all the grace of a bear in ballet shoes. The tea was thick, bitter, and wonderfully strange. The sweet that preceded it, a small cake shaped like a hydrangea, was so beautiful that I felt it a crime to eat it, and I ate it anyway.

"The rain is good for the tea," said the hostess, through a young interpreter. "It makes us sit still."

I thought about that on the walk back, under my transparent umbrella, along a canal lined with willows, where a heron stood in the shallows with the stillness of a calligraphic stroke. The lanterns were coming on in the old wooden houses, and the reflections trembled in the wet street. It struck me that Kyoto's genius is not in its monuments, though they are magnificent, but in its instinct for the pause: the gate that makes you slow down, the garden that makes you look, the cup that makes you wait. I had come, like everyone, to see something. I left having learned, with some surprise, how to sit in the rain and be glad of it.

questions.question: What does tsuyu mean?
questions.answer: Plum rain, the rainy season in June.

questions.question: What is special about Ryōan-ji?
questions.answer: A rock garden of fifteen stones, of which only fourteen are visible from any position.

questions.question: What is Saihō-ji known for?
questions.answer: Its garden of more than a hundred kinds of moss.

questions.question: What did the writer learn?
questions.answer: To sit still in the rain and be glad of it.
